title: New Lawsuits Challenge Trump's Green Card Freeze on Applicants From 75 Countries
excerpt: A 130-plaintiff lawsuit filed in Washington this week accuses the State Department of unlawfully continuing its nationality-based suspension of immigrant visas, weeks after a New York judge struck the policy down as 'patently unlawful.'
body:
• A complaint filed Thursday in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia — more than 130 plaintiffs, from U.S. citizens petitioning for relatives to foreign nationals seeking employment-based green cards — argues the State Department's ongoing suspension of green cards for applicants from 75 countries violates the Administrative Procedure Act and the separation of powers.
  • The Catholic Legal Immigration Network is pressing a separate challenge in the Southern District of New York, arguing immigration law requires individual public-charge assessments, not a blanket withholding of visa decisions.
  • On August 21, Judge Jeannette A. Vargas ruled the 75-country freeze "patently unlawful" and vacated it nationwide, ordering visa refusals based solely on the policy to be reconsidered — though an appeal and stay request remain possible.
  • The freeze suits follow Monday's lawsuits by dozens of Democratic-led states, counties and cities in Manhattan federal court challenging a separate DHS public-charge rule, set to take effect Friday, that would let officers weigh food stamps and Medicaid against green-card applicants.

What's new

A federal lawsuit filed Thursday in Washington is the latest to attack the Trump administration's suspension of green cards for applicants from 75 countries. The complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia by Red Eagle Law, LC, for more than 130 plaintiffs, argues the ongoing suspension violates the Administrative Procedure Act and the separation of powers: the government has a mandatory duty to process visas within a reasonable time, the nationality-based pause came without reasoned explanation, and it encroaches on Congress's immigration power. Separately, the Catholic Legal Immigration Network is challenging the same freeze in the Southern District of New York, arguing the Immigration and Nationality Act demands individualized public-charge assessments, not blanket withholding of visa decisions.

Context & background

The State Department last month said it was halting immigrant visas for nationals of the 75 countries while it updates screening to identify applicants who might become a "public charge," with no stated end date — though adopted children of American parents later qualified for a National Interest Exception. The policy has already lost in court once: on August 21, U.S. District Judge Jeannette A. Vargas ruled in CLINIC v. Rubio that the freeze was "patently unlawful," finding nationality-based discrimination, exceeding Secretary of State Marco Rubio's authority, and forcing officers to refuse applicants they had already found eligible. She vacated the policy nationwide and ordered such refusals sent back for reconsideration. The ruling can still be appealed or paused.

A second front is already in litigation: Monday's two lawsuits in Manhattan federal court seek to block a separate DHS rule, effective Friday, that would let officers deny green cards to applicants using food stamps, Medicaid and other public benefits — reviving and expanding a 2019 first-term policy. A third pressure point is building: a USCIS memo last week declaring green-card approval inside the U.S. an "exceptional benefit" would force most applicants, including H-1B workers, to return to their home countries to finish processing — a memo Bloomberg Law notes is a likely target of legal challenges.

"Behind this case are families, loved ones, and communities who were harmed by a policy that blocked immigrant visas on a categorical basis."

— Sarah Wilson, Partner and Federal Litigation Practice Leader, Colombo & Hurd, co-counsel for the plaintiffs

Impact & analysis

For applicants caught in the freeze, the courtroom is now the real processing queue. The Vargas vacatur offers the clearest relief: refusals that rested solely on the nationality-based freeze must be re-adjudicated without it. But relief will not be instant — a large backlog, slow consular implementation, and the possibility of an appeal with a stay request stand in the way. The human stakes are visible in the plaintiffs' roster: Dr. Fernando Lizcano Losada, a Colombian endocrinologist preparing to continue breast-cancer research at Harvard Medical School, was refused a visa on the theory he might become a public charge.

Diaspora angle

Indian immigrants sit at the intersection of all three fronts — family-sponsored applicants waiting on consular processing, and H-1B workers pursuing green cards through adjustment of status, a process the USCIS memo would push back overseas except in extraordinary circumstances. For a community that files some of the largest volumes of employment-based petitions, each courtroom decision lands on real lives and real timelines.

What's next

Three clocks to watch: the D.C. lawsuit's early proceedings; whether the government appeals or seeks a stay of the August 21 vacatur; and Friday's effective date for the DHS public-charge rule against the two Manhattan lawsuits. A challenge to the USCIS adjustment-of-status memo is likely to join the docket soon.
